why: Tableau (most important view upper-left) and ODown (primary metrics most prominent) are yes/yes; Apple WWDC22 says titles as headings, which is not placement.
Elastic (title and value never hidden) and ODown (baseline comparisons) are yes/yes; Linear says no to pairing with context charts; CDC sparkline is about grouped sparklines.
Elastic (line chart for precise time series) and ODown (line for trends, bar for quantities) are yes/yes; Carbon and Apple say zero-axis and categories, not chart choice.
Carbon (zero axis), Apple WWDC22 (fix lower bound to 0), FT (ordered bars) and Nast (larger to smaller) are yes/yes across IBM, Apple, FT and Nast.
Data School and Carbon (labels directly, avoid legends) are yes/yes; Tufte describes sparklines only, so partly.
ODown (8% men, 0.5% women; colour-blind palettes), Atlassian (limit to 5-6 colours) and Laws of UX (not colour alone) are yes/yes across three organisations.
GOV.UK (numbers right-aligned), IBM Carbon (medium 40 default) and NN/g (sticky headers over one screen) are yes/yes across three organisations.
PatternFly (never a card for dense repetitive content) and Apple WWDC25 (list over grid) are yes/yes.
Baymard (result counts next to filters), PatternFly (applied filter labels) and Playfair (filter next to its view) are yes/yes across three organisations.
Stanford (show review dates), NN/g (last-updated indicator) and CDC (show data source) are yes/yes across three organisations.
W3C (1.1.1 text alternative for charts), Apple, NN/g (long description), Salesforce and Microsoft are yes/yes across five organisations; Carbon covers the title only partly.

No source is yes/yes/yes: DecisionLab and Growth.Design support the keep-the-default premise only partly; GoodUI's preselect claim is not on its page; Apple WWDC24 is about sensible defaults in games.
